    Inflow surge – what do high-inflow days look like?

    ℹ Info – how are the average, spread and surge days calculated?

    Goal: find the days when far more tickets than usual were created, then show what is different on those days (which values, hours and weekdays).

    1. Daily count. Every day in the date range gets the number of cases created that day (after the master / child filters). A day with no cases counts as 0. With Days counted = Mon–Fri only, Saturdays and Sundays are left out completely: their days and their cases are not used, so the average is lower than total cases ÷ days.

    2. Average = total cases on the counted days ÷ number of counted days.
    Example: 1,922 cases on 14 weekdays → 1,922 ÷ 14 = 137.3 tickets / day. (If 307 weekend cases were also added, 2,229 ÷ 14 = 159, but that would mix weekend cases into weekday days, so they are excluded.)

    3. Spread (standard deviation) = how far a normal day is from the average. For every day: take (day count − average), square it, add all the squares, divide by the number of days, then take the square root.
    Example with 5 days of 100, 120, 140, 160, 180: average 140; differences −40, −20, 0, +20, +40; squares 1600, 400, 0, 400, 1600; their average is 800; square root = 28.3. A small spread means days are all alike; a large spread means days vary a lot.

    4. Surge = above average + sets the surge line: average + multiplier × spread. Example: 137.3 + 0.5 × 44.5 = 159.5, so any day with more than 159.5 tickets is a surge day. Average uses the average itself as the surge line (multiplier 0), so every day above average is a surge day. A bigger multiplier (1, 1.5, 2 × spread) flags only bigger spikes; a smaller one flags more days.

    How is the spread (–) calculated for the data on screen? Each row is one counted day; the totals at the bottom give the spread.

    5. Uplift = average tickets per surge day ÷ average tickets per normal day, shown per value, hour and weekday to point out what drives the surge. Surge detection is weak with fewer than 14 days, so use a longer date range.

        Ticket details

        Resolution target in calendar hours per priority. A case counts as resolved once it is Resolved or Closed (Closed cases were auto-closed after 3 days with no customer reply, so the clock stops at the resolution time, not the closing time). It is Met if resolved within the target, otherwise Breached. An open case is Breached once its age passes the target and At risk after 80% of it. The pre-filled hours (High 4, Medium 24, Low 72) are only placeholders, so set them to match your SLA policy. Leave a priority empty to leave it out.
        In this source the clock stops while the case is in a paused status: only the time spent in other statuses (Open, New, In Progress…) counts against the target. A case resolved after 30 hours, of which 10 hours were Pending or Waiting on Third Party, is scored on 20 hours. The paused time is read from the case's Status history.

          Searches Salesforce directly (no date filter needed) and builds a date-wise audit trail: e-mails, posts and comments, activities (tasks / events) and field history such as status and owner changes, with an analysis of the case.
          Uses the Resolved date & time data already downloaded in the master filter (no Salesforce call). Pick the resolved dates, then the group; the agent list is filled from that group's resolved cases in those dates. Suggested cases are the ones most worth auditing: the longest-running compared with the group's average age, and high-priority ones. Click Audit on a case to open its full audit trail.
          Searches case subjects, descriptions, e-mails, posts and comments across all of Salesforce for the same issue. Resolved and closed cases are shown first, each with the solution that was given (last agent e-mail, public comment or post), the case number and the related e-mails and posts.
          Takes the tickets created in the selected dates (for example this month), builds keywords from each one (Observation / Resolution details when a post has them, otherwise subject, description and posts), then searches the tickets created in the look-back window before the From date (default 6 months) for the same issue. For every new ticket you see whether it recurred and the old tickets best keyword match first, each with the solution that was given.
